title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: A person in motion always invents a purpose for that motion. To be able to march a thousand miles, you must believe that something good awaits you at the end of those thousand miles. You need the prospect of a promised land to have the strength to keep moving.

For the French during their advance, the promised land had been Moscow. During their retreat, it was their homeland. But their homeland was too far away, and for someone traveling a thousand miles, it's absolutely necessary to set aside the final goal and tell yourself: 'Today I'll reach a place twenty-five miles ahead, where I'll rest for the night.' And during that first day's march, the resting place eclipses the ultimate destination and draws all your hopes and desires. The impulses felt by a single person are always magnified in a crowd.

For the French retreating along the old Smolensk road, the final goal—their homeland—was too remote. Their immediate goal was Smolensk, toward which all their desires and hopes, enormously intensified in the mass, propelled them onward. It wasn't that they knew plenty of food and fresh troops awaited them in Smolensk, nor were they told so (on the contrary, their officers and Napoleon himself knew that provisions there were scarce). But this was the only thing that could give them the strength to keep moving and endure their present suffering. So those who knew and those who didn't both deceived themselves and pushed on toward Smolensk as toward a promised land.

Reaching the highway, the French fled with astonishing energy and unheard-of speed toward their chosen goal. Besides the shared impulse that bound the entire French mass into one body and gave it a kind of energy, there was another force holding them together: their sheer numbers. As with the physical law of gravity, their enormous mass drew individual human atoms to itself. In their hundreds of thousands, they moved like an entire nation.

Each man wanted nothing more than to give himself up as a prisoner and escape the horror and misery. But on one hand, the gravitational pull of Smolensk drew every one of them in the same direction; on the other, an army corps can't surrender to a company. Though the French seized every opportunity to break away and surrender on the slightest decent pretext, such opportunities didn't always arise. Their very numbers and the speed of their movement made it not just difficult but impossible for the Russians to halt them. No mechanical force could hasten the process of decomposition beyond a certain point.
A lump of snow can't be melted all at once. There is a minimum time required, and no amount of heat can melt it faster. In fact, the more heat you apply, the harder the remaining snow becomes.

Of the Russian commanders, Kutuzov alone understood this. When the French army's flight along the Smolensk road became well established, what Konovnitsyn had foreseen on the night of the eleventh began to happen. Every senior officer wanted to distinguish himself—to cut off, seize, capture, and crush the French—and all clamored for action.
Kutuzov alone used all his power (and a commander in chief's power is very limited) to prevent an attack.

He couldn't tell them what we can say now: 'Why fight? Why block the road, losing our own men and inhumanely slaughtering miserable wretches? What's the point, when a third of their army has already melted away on the march from Moscow to Vyazma without a single battle?' But drawing on his years of wisdom, he told them what they could understand—about the golden bridge—and they laughed at him and slandered him, flinging themselves on, tearing at, and gloating over the dying beast.

Ermolov, Miloradovich, Platov, and others near the French at Vyazma couldn't resist their desire to cut off and smash two French corps. To inform Kutuzov of their intentions, they sent him a blank sheet of paper in an envelope.

And try as Kutuzov might to hold the troops back, the Russians attacked, trying to block the road. Infantry regiments, we are told, advanced with music playing and drums beating, and killed and lost thousands of men.
But they didn't cut off or capture anyone. The French army, closing ranks more tightly in the face of danger, continued to melt steadily away as it pursued its fatal path toward Smolensk.
